passage:
[1] Before Kessel Foundry can pour an iron valve body, somebody has to carve the shape out of wood. The second bay past the scale house belongs to Odile Bracht, whose bench turns out no parts, only a pattern, a wooden double of the part, pressed into damp sand to leave a hollow behind it. Half the patterns on her rack is older than the furnace.

[2] Wood, though, is not cut to the finished size. Iron leaves the ladle above two thousand degrees and cools gradually over the eleven hours a heavy casting sits in its sand, drawing in on itself the whole time. A pattern cut straight to the drawing would give back a valve body a hair too small, so Bracht cuts each one oversize and lets the cooling pull it to size.

[3] Gray iron draws in about an eighth of an inch per foot. Bronze shrinks, aluminum shrinks nearly twice as much as gray iron does. Bracht keeps a wooden shrink rule for each metal, a ruler whose inches are stretched by the allowance, so the oversize dimension reads straight off the drawing. Sizing a pattern without one would mean doing the arithmetic on every dimension, checking it against the drawing, and to weigh a scrapped pour against the hour saved.

[4] A pattern sized for gray iron is wrong for every other metal, and nothing on it shows which one it was cut for. Kessel's answer is a number burned into the back of each pattern: 1 for gray iron, 2 for bronze, 3 for aluminum, and nobody pulls one without reading it. Kessel has never set any of this down in a manual. Still, the only list of what the numbers mean is a strip of tape on the shops door.

[5] [A] A new alloy reaches the shop every few years, and the first pattern cut for one is sized from a guess. [B] Bracht takes the published figure for the nearest metal she pours, cuts the pattern to it, and waits. [C] The first casting out of that mold is measured cold, and the gap becomes the shop's own allowance. [D] A fourth rule hangs on her wall, cut in 2019 for a silicon bronze nobody upstate had a figure for.
prompt: In paragraph 1, which choice is most acceptable in place of "pattern,"?
explanation: What follows is a renaming of the same thing - "a wooden double of the part" - and a comma is the mark that attaches a nonrestrictive appositive of that kind, so "pattern," stands. "pattern;" would need an independent clause on both sides of it and has one on neither; "pattern:" would need an independent clause in front of it, and "whose bench turns out no parts" is a relative clause that cannot stand alone; and "pattern" with no mark at all runs the noun into its own renaming.
